scenario: AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She also has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can not afford it. This was confirmed by both the bully, and the friend. My daughter was silent on the way home and i informed her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get you in a lot of trouble. and that in the future she needs to speak to myself or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost her shit on me, in full tears, telling me that this is a one way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn’t want us to intervene. I am wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA?

My daughter is in sixth grade, and every morning I give her a couple of dollars for lunch money. Over the last few weeks, I noticed that I was missing a bit more money than usual. She also mentioned that she has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can't afford it. Both the bully and the friend confirmed this. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. Alright, so to figure this out, I need to consider several aspects: the immediate action of calling the police, the context of why my daughter was stealing, the reaction from my wife and daughter, and the potential long-term consequences of my actions. First, calling the police seems like a strong reaction, especially for a child in sixth grade. It's important to consider the intent behind this action. Was it to teach a lesson about stealing, or was there another motive? It seems like the primary intent was to teach a lesson, but the way it was done might have been too harsh. Next, understanding why my daughter was stealing is crucial. She mentioned that there was a bully stealing her lunch money and forcing her to buy lunch for the bully. She also mentioned helping a friend who couldn't afford lunch. This context is important because it shows that her actions were not simply about stealing for the sake of it but were influenced by external pressures and a desire to help others. The reaction from my wife and daughter indicates that my approach was not well-received. My wife was upset, feeling that this action could lead to estrangement from our daughter. My daughter was scared and felt that she had lost her friend because of the attention brought to her financial issue. She apologized and expressed that she didn't want us to intervene, which suggests that she felt cornered and misunderstood. Considering the long-term consequences, involving the police in this situation might have had a lasting negative impact on my daughter's trust in me and her willingness to come to me for help in the future. It could also have affected her relationship with her friends and her standing at school. Perhaps a better approach would have been to talk to my daughter first, understand why she was taking the money, address the underlying issues like the bullying and her desire to help her friend, and then decide on an appropriate way to teach her about the wrongfulness of stealing. This approach would have allowed for open communication, understanding, and a more supportive resolution. In summary, while the intent was to teach a lesson, the method used might have been too severe and didn't take into account the complexities of the situation. It's important to approach such issues with empathy, understanding, and open communication to foster trust and cooperation.
